old: Udātta, anudātta, and the pluta (prolated) accent are marked distinctly across the words to be recited. Those wishing to master pronunciation must study these markings closely. The udātta accent is marked with a vertical stroke above the letter; the svarita accent is marked below; the anudātta carries no mark at all — bare, unmarked letters are to be understood as anudātta. One must understand these markings letter by letter. Where the accent-mark sits — above the letter, at its foot, or beside it — determines the type of accent for that syllable. **As an example, here is a well-known mantra shown with its accent-marks in place**—
new: The udātta and prachaya accents are pronounced without any difference. When the anudātta is spoken, the syllable is pronounced lowered; when the svarita is pronounced, it is raised a little. In writing, the udātta and the prachaya accents carry no mark. But syllables that stand without a mark at the beginning of a mantra, and syllables that come without a mark after an anudātta, are to be understood as udātta syllables. The anudātta syllable is marked with a small horizontal stroke below the syllable; the svarita carries a small vertical stroke above the syllable. **As an example, one mantra is shown here with its accent-marks in place**—
basis: Kannada p.550: udatta and prachaya unmarked; anudatta marked by a small horizontal stroke below, svarita by a small vertical stroke above; unmarked syllables at the start and after an anudatta are udatta (English had the marks and the unmarked rule reversed)

old: **Meaning:** the letters pronounced with normal duration are called "hrasva" (short). This much is stated explicitly. In the second mātrā-length, a and ī and similar letters are prolonged, called "dīrgha" (long). Three-mātrā duration is called "pluta" (prolated), used specifically for calling out or summoning. Whether short, long, or prolated, in any given sentence, the mātrā (quantity) is determined by these three durations. Three-mātrā...
new: **Meaning:** the letter pronounced in the time taken to utter the vowel a is called hrasva (short); this is called one mātrā. Letters such as ā and ī, pronounced in the time of two mātrās, are called dīrgha (long). Letters pronounced in the time of three mātrās are called pluta (prolated). In the first example sentence the syllable is a pluta of three mātrās, and the numeral 3 is customarily written to show it; there is also a pluta of two mātrās, as in the second example sentence.
basis: Kannada pp.550-551: hrasva one matra, dirgha two, pluta three; the numeral 3 is written to show a three-matra pluta; a two-matra pluta also exists (English had pluta used for calling and omitted the 2-matra pluta)

old: (Sutra) — see page 548 above
new: (Sutra)

old: **This is a well-known cautionary tale.** Correctly pronounced, "indraśatru" should mean "he whose slayer is Indra" (a bahuvrīhi compound, accent on the first member) — but Tvashtri, in performing a sacrifice to create a son who would destroy Indra, mispronounced the accent, unintentionally shifting the compound's sense to a tatpuruṣa ("Indra's slayer") — and as a direct result, the very son born from that yajna was destroyed **by** Indra, rather than destroying him. This story is given in detail in works such as the same passage cited above (page 552) and in Panini's grammar tradition.
new: **This is a well-known cautionary tale.** If "indraśatru" is to mean "he who slays Indra", the compound must be a tatpuruṣa ("Indra's slayer"), and then its last syllable must carry the udātta accent. But the word in the mantra has the udātta on its first syllable, and the last syllable (tru) is not udātta; so it is a bahuvrīhi, meaning "he whose slayer is Indra", that is, one to be slain by Indra. Because of this change of accent the sense reversed: Tvashtri, who sacrificed to obtain a son who would slay Indra, obtained one who was slain by Indra, and harm came to him instead of the fruit.
basis: Kannada pp.552-553: tatpurusha needs the udatta on the last syllable; the mantra has it on the first, so the word is a bahuvrihi 'slain by Indra' (English had the roles reversed and added Panini's grammar tradition)

old: **"Bala"** refers to the place of articulation. The place refers to the specific effort involved in pronouncing a given letter; the letter pronounced with the appropriate effort at its proper place is called "sthāna" (station). "Kaṇṭha (throat), tālu (palate), danta (teeth), oṣṭha (lips)" and similar — these are the places at which the letters are articulated. According to the Anga tradition, the letter **a** [and similar vowels] are articulated in the throat; the semivowels [ya, ra, la, va] are articulated with slight contact — this is called "īṣat" (slight) contact. Understanding this proper application of contact and place, at each letter, matters for correct articulation.
new: **"Bala"** means the place and the effort of articulation. "Place" (sthāna) is the part of the mouth to which the tongue is applied when a letter is pronounced; the Śikṣā says there are eight places, throat, palate, teeth, lips and the like. The vowels (a and the rest) are untouched: in pronouncing them the tongue touches no part of the mouth. The semivowels (ya, ra, la, va) are "īṣat" (slightly) touched. This manner of pronouncing a letter by touching the tongue to the palate and the other parts of the mouth is called "effort" (prayatna).
basis: Kannada p.551: vowels are aspashta (the tongue touches no part of the mouth), ya ra la va are ishat (slightly) spashta; prayatna = the manner of touching (English said vowels are articulated in the throat)

old: **"Sāma"** means: when reciting the words, neither shortening a short-duration letter nor lengthening it beyond its proper measure — this is the true meaning of correct recitation. One must recite with steady attentiveness, without letting the mind wander, taking care not to reverse the order of the letters, nor to omit any, nor mispronounce them. If one recites in a manner that adds extraneous sounds or drops necessary ones — the meaning of the words becomes muddled, and the recitation carries the fault of ill-effect (as the poison-anecdote and similar stories illustrate). Reciting evenly, without irregularity, is the virtue of proper "sāma."
new: **"Sāma"** (sāmya, uniformity) means that, in pronouncing words, rules such as which letter is to be recited short and which long make the word uniform. One must not recite too hastily, nor drag out the letters too slowly. Without such faults, the words must be pronounced clearly and sweetly to the ear (audibly). This manner of pronunciation is called "sāmya".
basis: Kannada p.551: sama = samya, no too-hasty and no too-slow recitation, clear and audible (English added reversed letters, omitted letters, extraneous sounds and the poison anecdote)

old: ### On "Santāna" (Madhurya) — Joining
new: ### On "Madhurya" (Sweetness)
basis: Kannada p.551: the quality quoted (Shi. 3-3) is madhurya; santana is a separate head on p.552

old: **Santāna** refers to the proper procedure for joining words together, according to the rules of euphonic combination (sandhi). "Vāyav" is a case of vāyu joined with "ā": when the word "vāyu" is followed by "ā" [as in "vāyav ā yāhi"], sandhi occurs. Similarly, "indrāgnī" is a case where "indra" and "agnī" combine: when "indra" is followed by "agnī," this particular sandhi results — which words combine, and how they combine, is set out in the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa). Since a full discussion of this belongs there, it is not elaborated in the Śikṣā, and is only briefly touched upon here.
new: **Santāna** means the arrangement of joining according to the rules of saṃhitā or sandhi. In the sentence "vāyav ā yāhi", vāyo + ā becomes vāyav ā by the change of o to av, and sandhi results. In the sentence "indrāgnī ā gatam", indrāgnī + ā gatam undergoes no sandhi at all, and the original form remains as it was. Since many such rules of sandhi are explained at length in the science of grammar, the Śikṣā leaves them aside without explaining them.
basis: Kannada p.552: indragni + a gatam undergoes no sandhi (English said indra and agni combine); the Siksha leaves sandhi aside (English added 'only briefly touched upon here')

old: **This same matter is explained by the mantra given in the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda** — see the fuller citation and resolution on the following page.
new: **This same matter is explained by the mantra given in the Taittiriya Samhita of the Yajurveda.**

old: ...is that this mantra needs to be understood as **"sākṣād indraśatru-varthārthasya"** — "one whose very slayer is directly Indra." When Tvashtri performed the yajna intending to produce a son who would slay Indra, he intended the compound "indraśatru" to mean "the slayer of Indra" (indraṃ śatruḥ — a tatpuruṣa compound: "Indra's foe"). But because he pronounced it with the *wrong accent* — properly accented, "indraśatru" as a **bahuvrīhi compound** must instead be understood to mean "he whose slayer is Indra" (indraḥ śatruḥ yasya saḥ — "one destroyed **by** Indra"). Accent alone determines this distinction.
new: What we need is the mantra "svāhendraśatrur vardhasva". When Tvashtri Prajapati performed the sacrifice, intending to obtain a son who would slay Indra, and made the offering in the fire, the accent of the word "indraśatru" was changed and the sense changed with it: instead of "the son who slays Indra" it became "the son who is slain by Indra", and harm came instead of the fruit. Let us consider how the change of accent came about. For "indraśatru" to mean the son who slays Indra, it would have to be a tatpuruṣa compound ("Indra's slayer"), and its last syllable would then have to be udātta. But the word used in the mantra has the udātta on its first syllable, and the last syllable (tru) is not udātta. So the word is a bahuvrīhi instead of a tatpuruṣa, and the meaning changes accordingly.
basis: Kannada p.553: tatpurusha needs final udatta; the mantra word is initial-udatta, hence bahuvrihi 'slain by Indra' (English had a different, garbled account)

old: Because of this single mispronunciation, the very meaning of the mantra reversed: instead of producing a destroyer *of* Indra, the sacrifice produced a being destined to be destroyed *by* Indra — and that is precisely what happened, as the sacred narrative recounts. This shows how essential correct accent is:
new: Because of this change of accent the sense of the mantra reversed: instead of producing a slayer of Indra, the sacrifice produced one to be slain by Indra, and the sacrificer received harm instead of the fruit. This shows how essential correct accent is:
basis: Kannada p.553: the son would be one slain by Indra, harm came to the sacrificer (English said a being destined to be destroyed by Indra 'as the narrative recounts' and put the compound-types in the wrong order)

old: **Meaning:** the compound "indraśatru," when correctly accented as a bahuvrīhi (with acute accent on the first member), means "he whose enemy/destroyer is Indra." Because Tvashtri's actual pronunciation shifted the accent to the pattern proper to a tatpuruṣa compound, the sense inadvertently reversed to "the destroyer of Indra" — and the resulting confusion in meaning led directly to his own destruction, as the story shows. **From this, it becomes clear how essential correct knowledge of accent truly is.** This example alone suffices to demonstrate why the Śikṣā treatise is indispensable.
new: **Meaning:** if "indraśatru" is a tatpuruṣa, it means "slayer of Indra" and has the udātta on its last syllable; the word in the mantra has the udātta on its first syllable and is therefore a bahuvrīhi, "he whose slayer (śatru) is Indra", that is, one to be slain by Indra. By this change of accent the sense reversed and, instead of the fruit, harm came to the sacrificer. **From this it is clear how essential correct knowledge of the Śikṣā is for avoiding such faults of accent, letters and the like.**
basis: Kannada p.553: roles of slayer and slain were reversed in the English (it said the accent shifted to the tatpurusha pattern and the son destroyed Tvashtri)

old: **Meaning:** for this daily brahma-yajña, one must recite according to the sequence in which the mantras are collected within the Samhita — not according to when each mantra is actually employed in a rite. The order of recitation for the brahma-yajña follows the Samhita's own internal arrangement: the mantras belonging to the trees and plants (used for consecrating the sacred grass and similar purposes) are recited according to that fixed textual order, not according to their scattered ritual usage.
new: **Meaning:** in this brahma-yajña japa, the mantras beginning with the first Rik of the Saṃhitā are to be recited in the order in which they stand in the Saṃhitā. Likewise, at the vācaḥ-stoma sacrifice, in which all the Riks, all the Yajus mantras and all the Sāman mantras are to be recited, the order given by the traditional authorities is to be accepted.
basis: Kannada p.556: brahmayajna japa follows the Samhita order; likewise the vacah-stoma sacrifice follows the order of those who know the tradition (English had trees, plants and sacred grass, which are not in the Kannada)

old: **This same principle** — that recitation-order and ritual-employment-order are two entirely separate matters — resolves the apparent contradiction: since Ashvalayana's Kalpa-sutra text (dealing with actual ritual sequence) doesn't follow the Rigveda-Samhita's own textual order, this in no way undermines the claim that the Samhita's own arrangement is fixed for the purposes of daily recitation (svādhyāya) and the brahma-yajña specifically.
new: The Mantra-kāṇḍa (the Saṃhitā) is thus arranged for japa in the brahma-yajña and the like, not for showing the order of performing sacrifices; therefore, although the order of the Mantra-kāṇḍa is not found in Āśvalāyana's Kalpa-sūtra, there is no contradiction in it.
basis: Kannada p.556: the mantra-kanda order is for japa, not for the performance of sacrifices, so its absence in the Kalpa-sutra is no contradiction (English had a different argument)

old: **One further doubt might arise:** does Ashvalayana's own Grihya-sutra, in laying down the rules for daily recitation, follow the mantra order of the Rigveda-Samhita, or does it follow some other principle? — Whichever the answer, one thing is beyond dispute: a person should recite his own portion, be it Rig, Yajur, or Sama, according to a fixed and definite sequence.
new: The same traditional order is to be followed wherever the whole Mantra-kāṇḍa is employed, as in the recitation prescribed as an expiation.
basis: Kannada p.556: in the recitation of the Veda as expiation and in the use of the mantras the traditional order is followed (English invented a doubt about the Grihya-sutra)

old: **Wherever employment [of a mantra in ritual] is explicitly commanded, the traditional [Samhita] order need not be followed** — this is not to be regarded as a genuine flaw. In the case of works belonging to different Shakhas, understanding the specific application (viniyoga) of each mantra requires study of those Shakhas' own Kalpa-sutra texts.
new: **If it be asked** why uses are stated for mantras that are not in the Rigveda Saṃhitā, this is no fault. The use established in another Brāhmaṇa for mantras recited in another Śākhā has to be stated here by the principle of gathering together the qualities (guṇopasaṃhāra-nyāya). The logicians say that one rite rests on all the Śākhās; therefore Kalpa, like Śikṣā, is needed.
basis: Kannada pp.554-555: the objection about mantras not in the Samhita is answered by the gunopasamhara principle (English had a different statement about explicit commands)

old: Now, this discussion is undertaken by those wishing to critically examine the works composed by the various Angas. **Kalpa** means the treatises that treat the specific methods for performing yajnas — that is, the works explaining ritual procedure (karma), mantra-application (viniyoga), and the substances to be used (dravya) in a yajna. Among the ancient works of this kind, Ashvalayana, Apastamba, and Baudhayana are well-known, and among more recent works, Katyayana and similar authors have composed treatises. There are many such Kalpa-treatises belonging to different Shakhas — Shrauta-sutra, Grihya-sutra, Dharma-sutra, Paribhasha-sutra, and so on. **Among these, we shall now examine an objection raised regarding Ashvalayana's Shrauta-sutra specifically**—
new: So far the Vedānga Śikṣā has been dealt with; now the books of Kalpa, the sūtra-works, are examined. Kalpa means the works that set out the rules for performing sacrifices, the application (viniyoga) of mantras and the order of performing the sacrifice. They were composed in sūtra form by great sages such as Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba and Bodhāyana. For the Rigveda the Kalpa-sūtras composed by Āśvalāyana are the chief ones; for the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, Āpastamba, Bodhāyana and others composed Kalpa-sūtras; the other Vedas and other Śākhās also have Kalpa-sūtras composed by other sages. This has already been explained in detail (see page 32). According to the rites the sūtra-works are of many kinds: Śrauta-sūtra, Gṛhya-sūtra, Dharma-sūtra, Paribhāṣā-sūtra and so on. Of these the Śrauta-sūtra is the chief, so we shall examine it here. **In composing his Śrauta-sūtra, what order did Āśvalāyana follow?**
basis: Kannada p.555: ancient authors named are Ashvalayana, Apastamba, Bodhayana (English added 'more recent Katyayana'); Kannada refers to p.32, which the English lacked; kinds of sutra-works as in Kannada

old: Do Ashvalayana's followers, in the Shrauta-sutra, follow the order employed in the ritual-application of the mantras, following the sequence in which they occur in the Samhita? Or do they follow some other order not matching the Kanda (section) division? Whatever it may be, they do not follow the Samhita's own Mantra-kanda sequence at all. If it be objected that in one instance, at least, the order matches — namely, where it is said—
new: Did he follow the order of the Mantra-kāṇḍa (the mantras used in the sacrifice), or the order given in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa? He did not follow the first. At the beginning of his work he opens the section on the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice, saying—
basis: Kannada p.555: he follows neither the mantra-kanda nor the Aitareya Brahmana order, since he begins with the Darsha-Purnamasa (English put it as a doubt about an objection)

old: (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1-1-3) — this is [merely] because the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice comes first in the sequence of sacrificial rites, [not because it follows the Samhita's mantra-order]. The word **"agnihotra"** begins their treatise likewise — the mantra collection for Agnihotra is not found gathered anywhere in the Samhita as a coherent block. Therefore, the Kalpa-treatises follow their *own* sequence, based on the order of ritual performance, not the Samhita's own arrangement. Precisely because these two orderings can differ, one's own Brahmana-portion may not follow the same sequence either. Some might say — but the text opens—
new: (Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1-1-3). The mantras at the beginning of the Rigveda Saṃhitā, such as the first Rik, are nowhere used in the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice; therefore the order of the Mantra-kāṇḍa was not followed. Did he follow the second, the order of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa? That too is not so. For at the beginning of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa come the mantras connected with the dīkṣaṇīyā rite, as in the passage—
basis: Kannada p.555: Agnimile etc. are not used in the Darsha-Purnamasa; the Brahmana begins with the dikshaniyeshti (English had an invented 'agnihotra' beginning and a different argument)

new: At the dikshaniya sacrifice they offer the purodasa cake in eleven platters

old: **Here a special doubt must be resolved.** In the Mantra-kanda (the portion of the Samhita comprising mantras, including the Khilas), determining which mantra decisively belongs to which rite is often difficult — the composer of the Brahmana-portion doesn't reveal this explicitly. The performer of the Brahma-yajna needs no such determination. **The Brahma-yajna's injunction is stated thus:**

basis: Kannada p.556: the mantra-kanda is ordered for japa in brahmayajna etc., not for the order of performing sacrifices (English invented a doubt about determining mantras for rites)

Without knowing this precise application, one cannot perform the rites correctly. Therefore, it is entirely proper to first know the sequence of ritual acts and only afterward identify the mantras belonging to each — an entirely different concern from the Samhita's own arrangement. It has also been said elsewhere—

Since the ordering of a given rite draws upon whatever [texts] are genuinely applicable [to it], it is entirely proper to follow that rite's own [functional] order [rather than the Samhita's].

Since that order is in the Veda itself, it is natural that the same order is followed in japa, recitation and the like.

old: **Followers of Ashvalayana** established their own Kalpa-sutra in accordance with the order of the Darsha-Purnamasa rite. The word "aitareya" appears at the very beginning of their Brahmana. That the Brahmana thus follows the order of the Darsha-Purnamasa rite, rather than the Samhita's own arrangement, should present no obstacle at all. And it has already been shown (see previous discussion) that followers of Ashvalayana also, in composing their own Kalpa-sutra, followed the Darsha-Purnamasa rite's own sequence. **Since the Kalpa Anga's genuine purpose is precisely to explain the application (viniyoga) of the mantras, this establishes the usefulness of studying the Kalpa Anga.**
new: **Ashvalayana** begins his Kalpa-sutra with the Darsha-Purnamasa sacrifice. In the Aitareya Brahmana the dīkṣaṇīyā rite is stated first. But since the dīkṣaṇīyā rite is a modification of the Darsha-Purnamasa, and it is proper to state the model rite first and the modification afterwards, Ashvalayana was right to state the Darsha-Purnamasa first. (The matter of model rites and modifications has been explained earlier.) **Therefore, since the Kalpa-sutras, by stating the application of mantras, teach the order of performing the sacrifice, they are of service.**
basis: Kannada p.557 (English had 'the word aitareya appears at the very beginning' and an unsupported argument)

old: Now let us critically examine the grammatical discussion that stands as the principal matter among the Veda's Angas. Grammar accepts and orders the roots (prakṛti), suffixes (pratyaya), word-forms, and their meaning-determinations in the appropriate contexts where they apply. As it was said before, this too has its basis in the **Aindravāyavagraha-brāhmaṇa**—

basis: Kannada p.563: the gods agreed; the offering is taken together in a single homa (English added 'both deities accepted the offering')

old: **Grammar itself was, in ancient times, composed in the earliest period — vast in extent, like the ocean itself.** The roots, suffixes, words, and sentences were originally undivided (agrantha, unarranged into a systematic textual form). Then, out of desire for the fulfillment [of ritual duties], the gods approached Indra alone specifically, and by combining the powers of Vayu and Soma-Rasa-graha with him, established a fixed order — and thus, from that point on, this speech came to be arranged in a systematic, divided fashion, namely: words, roots, and suffixes, distinguished from one another. **Because of this, the wisest sages, from Pāṇini onward, arranged this speech (that is, established a grammatical treatise) in a fixed, methodical form — this is the understood significance here.**
new: **In ancient times a text like "agnim īḷe purohitam" was an undivided sound, like the roar of the sea, without the divisions of root, suffix, word and sentence.** Then Indra, requested by the gods and pleased with the boon that he and Vayu might take the soma juice in one vessel, separated that undivided Speech in the middle and established the divisions such as root and suffix throughout. **So this Speech, analysed (vyākṛta) by Pāṇini and other great sages by the rules of grammar, is recited by all — this is the sense.**
basis: Kannada p.563: the undivided speech was divided by Indra; Panini and others analysed it (English said grammar itself was composed in the earliest period and the gods approached Indra alone)

old: Regarding what specific purpose this Grammar serves, later scholars, in their own tradition, have stated—
new: What the use of this Grammar is, Vararuchi has shown in his Vārtika—
basis: Kannada p.564: Vararuchi in his Vartika (English said 'later scholars, in their own tradition')

old: Vararuchi has clearly set out these five purposes in his own vārtika-treatise.
new: Patañjali has explained these purposes, and others, clearly in his Mahābhāṣya.
basis: Kannada p.564: Patanjali explained the uses in the Mahabhashya; Vararuchi only listed them

old: **Rakṣā (Protection):** since Vedic mantras have come down through the ages, doubts arise concerning whether their forms have been corrupted, whether some deviation has crept into the words as transmitted. Precisely to remove such doubts and to protect the Veda's genuine form from corruption, Grammar is necessary. Without knowing Grammar, one cannot distinguish which letters, among those forming a word, are genuinely correct and which have been altered — nor determine, through Grammar's principles, the correct application of the mantras. Hence, without knowledge of Grammar, one cannot properly identify errors of accent, wrong letters, and similar deviations.
new: **Rakṣā (Protection):** Grammar is to be studied in order to protect the Vedas, that is, to preserve the Vedic texts as they are, so that they are not altered by pronunciation and the like and no variant readings or losses arise. One who knows the changes of letters caused by loss, addition and the like will keep the Vedas intact, and such a grammarian can understand the Veda well.
basis: Kannada p.564 (English had doubts about corrupted mantras and application of mantras)

old: **Ūha (Adaptation):** the words found in the Vedic mantras — nouns, verbs, and similar forms — are not always used explicitly in their fully expanded application; often, the application must be inferred and understood [i.e., adapted to the specific ritual context]. This too requires proficiency in Grammar. Where the mantras must be modified [in case, number, gender] for ritual employment — this adaptation likewise cannot be accomplished without knowledge of Grammar.
new: **Ūha (Adaptation):** In the Vedic mantras the genders, numbers, cases and the like are not used so strictly; and at the sacrifice the mantras have to be used with some change of number, case and the like to suit the occasion. One who does not know Grammar cannot make such changes. So that one may know which number and which case to supply on each occasion, Grammar must be studied.
basis: Kannada p.564

old: **Āgama (Scriptural Priority):** the Brahmin who desires knowledge must study and understand not only the Veda itself, but also the dharma expressed through its established, systematic form — this too the shastras declare. Among the six Angas of the Veda, Grammar holds the foremost place. Effort spent studying this principal Anga will prove fruitful. Therefore, Grammar should be studied.
new: **Āgama (Scripture):** The scriptures say that a brahmin, without desiring any reward, must study the Veda with its six Angas, which is of the nature of dharma, and must understand its meaning. Among the six Vedāngas Grammar is the chief. Effort spent on studying this chief Anga is fruitful. Therefore Grammar must be studied.
basis: Kannada p.564

old: **Lāghava (Brevity):** to know the Veda with genuine ease, one must study Grammar. Once, when the sage Brihaspati desired to teach the science of words to Indra, he explained it word by word — an approach that even after a thousand celestial years, remained incomplete. Grammar's own systematic method (through its structured rules on roots, suffixes, and the like) accomplishes in a single stroke what such an exhaustive word-by-word approach never could.
new: **Lāghava (Ease):** Grammar is to be studied so that the Veda may be understood easily. Once Brihaspati, the teacher of the gods, tried to teach Indra the science of words, and taught the peculiarities of the form and derivation of each word in the Veda for a thousand years by the divine reckoning; yet he did not reach the end. The teacher was Brihaspati, the learner Indra, and the time a thousand divine years; still it was not finished. Nowadays the longest life of a man is about a hundred years; how could he learn the science of words by taking each word in turn? Therefore Grammar must be studied so that the use of words may be learned easily and quickly.
basis: Kannada pp.564-565: laghu = ease of understanding (English said brevity, 'in a single stroke')

old: **Sandeha (Removal of Doubt):** even one who knows how to distinguish between correct and incorrect forms may occasionally have doubts about a particular word's status. If, at such a time, one lacks the ability to apply Grammar's rules, one cannot resolve the doubt.
new: **Sandeha (Removal of Doubt):** When the right meaning of words is to be fixed, many doubts arise. Grammar must be studied to remove them.
basis: Kannada p.565

old: —(great and spotted — meaning a bull that is both great and spotted)? Or as a karmadhāraya compound meaning "the great-spotted-one"?
new: — (a karmadhāraya compound, "she who is both great and spotted")? Or as a bahuvrīhi compound, "she whose spots are great"?
basis: Kannada p.565: karmadharaya 'great and spotted' versus bahuvrihi 'she whose spots are great' (English had a bull)

old: **This kind of doubt-resolution is Grammar's chief use.** Therefore, Grammar should be studied to remove such doubts.
new: In a karmadhāraya the two words are independent, with no relation of qualifier and qualified; in a bahuvrīhi the whole compound qualifies another, principal word ("she whose spots are great"); so the two analyses give different meanings. Therefore Grammar must be studied to remove such doubts.
basis: Kannada p.565 (English added 'Grammar's chief use')

old: The sutras of these [purposes] are as follows:
new: Besides these, Grammar has many further uses; they are stated in sūtra form and each is explained at length. These sūtras are:
basis: Kannada p.565: further uses, stated in sutra form (English said the sutras of these five purposes)

old: **Devāsurāḥ (Gods and Asuras):** it is said that in ancient times, gods and demons — belonging to the same lineage — became rivals for supremacy over the three worlds. Then, both sides ("devāḥ" and "asuraḥ")...
new: **Te'surāḥ (The Asuras):** those demons, at one time (in battle), pronounced a wrong word and were therefore defeated. Instead of shouting the cry "he 'rayo he 'rayah" (O enemies!),
basis: Kannada p.565: the daityas lost the battle by a wrong word (English had gods and asuras of the same lineage rivals for the three worlds)

old: (In place of the letter "l" [in certain dialectal pronunciations, sounds shift]) — using "r" in place of "l" pronounces "layaḥ" as "rayaḥ" ("layaḥ" = destruction; "rayaḥ" = wealth) — and speaking this way, if "layaḥ" (destruction) is [mistakenly] spoken as "layaḥ" (with a corrupted, garbled sound), it becomes offensive to a brahmin's ears. That is why one should avoid speaking corrupted speech (mleccha-speech). And that "corrupted speech" (apaśabda) itself is precisely what must not be uttered — a corrupted word must be studiously avoided; Grammar should therefore be studied specifically to avoid such corrupted speech.
new: they pronounced l in place of r and said "helayo helayah" (layah = destruction); so they met with laya, that is, destruction and defeat. Therefore a brahmin must not become a mleccha, that is, he must not speak a corrupt word as the mlecchas do; a corrupt word is itself mleccha. Grammar should be studied so as not to utter such corrupt words.
basis: Kannada p.566: they used l for r (English had r for l, and 'offensive to a brahmin's ears')

old: Whether wrong in accent or wrong in letter — a word used incorrectly does not convey its intended meaning at all. Whether the fault lies in accent or arises through incorrect meaning, this indicates a corrupted word. This shows the meaning being conveyed as fault-bearing. Because of this defective usage, [the mantra] harms the sacrificer, just as we've seen, in a similar manner, with the "indraśatru" example — [it] causes the yajamāna to be struck down. From this discussion, we've seen the various flaws that can arise. Therefore, to avoid producing a corrupted word, one must study Grammar.
new: If in a word the accent or a letter is lost or changed, it is a corrupted word (duṣṭa śabda). Such a use of a word does not convey the intended meaning but speaks a wrong one. Therefore the use of a corrupted word brings harm to the sacrificer, as a thunderbolt strikes an enemy. The word "indraśatru" used with a changed accent is the example. Therefore, to avoid such faults, that is, to avoid using a corrupted word, Grammar should be studied.
basis: Kannada p.566

old: **"Yas tu Prayuṅkte"** (He Who Rightly Applies It) — [regarding] the use of words, and the skill applied in a given context; how one should properly apply each — this is what one must know. On this matter, the authors of the Kaśikā and similar grammatical treatises say—
new: **"Yas tu Prayuṅkte"** (He Who Rightly Applies It) — Grammar is to be studied in order to know how words are to be used on each occasion. On this the sage Katyayana says—
basis: Kannada p.566: Katyayana says (English attributed it to the authors of the Kasika)

old: **Meaning:** one who has skillfully mastered the proper use of speech, applying it correctly according to worldly needs, attains victory in the beyond as well. But one who is ignorant of the proper joining and application of speech is contaminated by corrupted forms (apaśabda).
new: **Meaning:** the wise man who, in the performance of rites as in worldly dealings, uses faultless good words as the occasion requires, gains fame in this world and endless victory (the best state) in the next world. But one who knows the right use of words, if he uses corrupt words, will not escape harm.
basis: Kannada p.567: it is the knower of word-use who is harmed by corrupt words (English said the ignorant one is contaminated)

old: **Here it must be understood what constitutes the "fault" of a corrupted word's use.** Concerning this: is the use of a corrupted word — that is, an improper word — itself a fault? Or does merely knowing that a word is corrupted, without actually using it, also become fault? Precisely because of this discussion, using a corrupted word is a true dharma-violation. In that sense, whether from mere knowledge of a corrupted word or from actually using it, an adharma (or, indeed, a sin) results. Ordinarily, corrupted forms are far more numerous than correct forms. Corrupted forms exist in great abundance. **For example — "gauḥ" (cow) — and its many corrupt variations, such as "gāvī," "goṇī," "gopotalikā," and similar, are widely known.**
new: **Who is harmed here? The one who knows the right use of words.** Why is harm done to one who knows? Because such a man can tell a good word from a bad one; if, with that knowledge, he still uses a corrupt word, what is it but harm? From good use of words dharma arises; in the same way from the use of corrupt words adharma, that is, sin, arises. Or: if, though he knows, he uses a corrupt word, a greater sin comes to him. Ordinarily good words (correct words that are not corrupt) are very few; corrupt words are the more numerous. Every word has many corrupt forms. For example the word "gauḥ" (cow) has many corrupt forms in common use, such as "gāvī," "goṇī," "gopotalikā."
basis: Kannada p.567 (English had the question of the fault of a corrupt word in a different sense)

old: Once, a certain man, from lack of grammatical knowledge, is said to have used a corrupted form without even knowing it was corrupted. If asked, can he escape blame simply because he acted out of ignorance rather than deliberate intent? — even so, ignorance is customarily excused as a defense. Whether or not a brahmin knew, if he committed some transgression, or created some fault through incorrect performance, does he not still bear consequences for it? Similarly, even one who commits a mistaken utterance without knowing it — precisely because he lacks the knowledge to know that his usage is corrupt — such a person does not incur the fault of adharma. **This shows why "avidvāṃsaha" (ignorance) is discussed** — merely knowing many words and their applications, without also knowing dharma, still leaves one properly usable in speech.
new: Someone may say that he used corrupt words from ignorance, that is, without knowing, because he had no knowledge of grammar. But to plead ignorance in this way is wrong, and it must not be done. If a man, without knowing it, kills a brahmin or drinks wine, does he not become an outcast even though he did it from ignorance? So, whether done knowingly or from ignorance, bad deeds do not escape punishment. In the same way, one who does not know the use of words and, in his ignorance, uses corrupt words does not escape adharma. And the one who knows the use of words and, by the strength of his knowledge, uses good words will surely gain dharma; since he has the knowledge, he should use good words only.
basis: Kannada p.567: ignorance is no excuse, the ignorant user of corrupt words does not escape adharma (English said such a person does not incur the fault)

old: **Meaning:** in this verse (which appears in the first chapter, describing the ordinary applications typically found), it is said that when responding to a salutation, one's own [family or personal] name should be pronounced with a lengthened vowel [as a mark of grammatical propriety]. Those unlearned people who do not know this rule instead pronounce it in an ordinary manner, as one would when addressing a woman [informally]. This is spoken of here as an example of erroneous practice. In this way, in a person's daily life as well, such improper practices are known to occur. This shows that even after studying and gaining scholarly proficiency, without also thoroughly mastering Grammar, one cannot avoid this kind of fault in ordinary word-usage. Since even scholars versed in the shastras are exposed to this risk, Grammar's importance is beyond dispute; without knowledge of Grammar, no genuine honour attaches [to one's learning]. **Therefore, Grammar should be studied.**
new: **Meaning:** as said in this verse, when a young student (vaṭu) salutes, he states his pravara (the names of the chief sages of his gotra) and salutes with "I, sir, salute you". The one saluted blesses the student by saying "Long life to you, Devadatta, may you prosper", pronouncing the last syllable of the student's name with a pluta of three mātrās. When he salutes an unlearned man who does not know how to bless with the pluta, the one who has gone away and returned must salute without reciting the pravara and the rest, simply saying "I salute", as he would salute women. Since such is the rule, to receive salutations in a learned assembly and the like one must be learned through the study of Grammar and the other sciences; an unlearned man receives no such honour. Therefore, to win honour, Grammar should be studied.
basis: Kannada p.568: the salutation rule (English made the saluted man pronounce his own name with a lengthened vowel and invented ordinary pronunciation as to a woman)

old: **"Vibhaktiṃ Kurvanti"** (They Perform the Division) — the priests who properly know the words to be recited (that is, the principal words belonging to the yajna, and the words belonging to that portion) must be studied for their correct application. Without knowledge of Grammar, this precept cannot be properly complied with. For this reason too, Grammar should be studied.
new: **"Vibhaktiṃ Kurvanti"** (They Adapt the Case-endings) — those who know the order of performing the sacrifice say that the prayājas must be made "with case-endings", that is, in reciting the prayāja mantras (the prayājas are the principal offering-mantras of the sacrifice) the case-endings must be adapted to the occasion so that the meaning fits. Without a knowledge of Grammar one cannot recite the prayāja mantras with the right case-endings. Therefore Grammar should be studied.
basis: Kannada p.568

old: this well-known text of the Rig Veda declares that whoever fully knows word, accent, and letter — one must know these matters, distinguishing each accent, each letter, in due order—
new: the man who is able to divide the Vedic sentences word by word, and the accents and letters at the pauses according to the rules of svara-sandhi—
basis: Kannada pp.568-569 (the text is a grammar sutra; English called it a well-known text of the Rig Veda)

old: the Nirukta gives the following example
new: we give the following example from the Rigveda
basis: Kannada p.569: 'Here we give an example. In the Rigveda' (English attributed the example to the Nirukta)

old: (see page 401)
new: (see page 40)
basis: Kannada p.569: (40 ne pustha); number from the Kannada

old: Ancient scholars have explained this mantra's meaning in various ways, according to whichever deity is taken as primary in the intended sense; even in our own tradition, this mantra has been interpreted in several distinct ways. **Grammatically, they explain the meaning as follows** —
new: Following the view of the Nirukta-authors, Agni, in the form of the sacrifice, is the chief deity; and since the sun, like Agni, is luminous, this mantra is said to speak of both, and Sayana has explained the meaning in his commentary accordingly. Those who know Grammar say that this mantra refers to the Word-Brahman (shabda-brahman). In the same way many others explain it in many ways. **The following is the way the grammarians explain the meaning** —
basis: Kannada p.570: Sayana's bhashya follows Nirukta (Agni and Surya), the grammarians say shabda-brahman (English had a vague statement about deities)

old: past (bhūta), present (bhavat), and future (vartamāna)
new: past (bhūta), future (bhaviṣyat), and present (vartamāna)
basis: Kannada p.570: bhuta, bhavishyat, vartamana = past, future, present

old: the great deity, referring to the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa) itself.
new: the great god, that is, the Word-Brahman (shabda-brahman).
basis: Kannada p.570: mahodevah = the great one, of the nature of shabda-brahman

old: That great deity — namely Grammar itself — has entered into mortal beings [i.e., speakers] and dwells within them.
new: That is, Grammar should be studied so that we may attain union (identity) with that great god.
basis: Kannada p.570: 'aviveshah' = may we have union with the great god, so one must study grammar

old: **This particular verse too has been explained in various ways by many scholars — differing interpretations arise from the differing systems each scholar follows.** In deciding its precise meaning, various learned authorities have explained the matter in different ways—
new: **This verse too has been explained in many ways by many commentators. In the Nirukta-pariśiṣṭa, in expounding this mantra, it is said that many scholars have explained the four divisions of speech in various ways—**
basis: Kannada p.571

old: **Om-kāra** (the syllable Om, the "praṇava") **is the great, non-decaying, imperishable [primal sound]. Nāma** (name) is called "bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ" — the vyāhṛti-forms, said to number four. **Nāma** (noun), **ākhyāta** (verb), **upasarga** (preposition), **nipāta** (particle) — these are the four kinds of speech, according to Vyākaraṇa's own account.
new: **The four classes of speech are, according to the seers (ṛṣis), the syllable Om together with the three vyāhṛtis "bhūḥ," "bhuvaḥ," "svaḥ"; according to the grammarians, noun (nāma), verb (ākhyāta), preposition (upasarga) and particle (nipāta);**
basis: Kannada p.571 (English had a garbled enumeration)

old: **Mantra, kalpa, vyākaraṇa, lokakṣaṇa-vyāhāra** — the [four-part] division as understood by ordinary human beings is one view. **Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Vyāvahārika-bhāṣā** (practical/ordinary speech) — this is another classification. **Sparśa, sparśī, kramīkṛta** and the "**vyāvahārikī**" (practical) speech — such is another accepted account.
new: **according to the performers of sacrifice (yājñikas), mantra, kalpa, grammar and the language people use in worldly dealings; according to the Nirukta-authors, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda and the language of worldly dealings; according to some (those who study the elements of nature), the speech of serpents, of birds and of small creeping creatures, together with the language of worldly dealings; and according to the upholders of the Self (ātma-pravādins), the speech found in cattle, in birds, in beasts and in man.**
basis: Kannada p.571: the classifications are attributed to the rishis, grammarians, yajnikas, nairuktas, some, and atma-pravadins (English attributed the second to 'ordinary human beings')

old: **Paśyantī, madhyamā, and vaikharī** — [along with a fourth] — these terms are used by some scholars to explain the fourfold division.
new: **In this way many have explained it in many ways.**
basis: Kannada p.571 has no pashyanti, madhyama, vaikhari or sparsha classification; addition removed

old: **In this way, the ancients have set forth many kinds of interpretation** — brahmins, wise in mind, know all these fourfold divisions. Of these four, three remain hidden and unmoving in their secret place; it is only the fourth portion of speech that ordinary humans commonly utter — this much is the accepted meaning, held by many across different systems.
new: **The main sense is this:** words are divided into four kinds, and all of them are known to intelligent brahmins. Of these four groups of words, three lie hidden in the cave and do not move, that is, being concealed they are not perceived by anyone; the fourth division, the web of words, is in use among men, and this men call speech. Here "manīṣiṇaḥ" means those who are able to understand by deliberating well in the mind, that is, the intelligent.
basis: Kannada p.571

old: **The meaning of the word "muktārtha"** [liberated/complete sense] is that speech has four distinct kinds. Grasping this well, brahmins who genuinely know [this doctrine] understand: among these four kinds of speech-categories, in three of them exist countless forms — but in only one does the ordinary usage practiced by human beings actually occur. That which remains, unspoken and unmoving in most cases, is what most people are unaware even exists. Here, the terms "manīṣiṇaḥ" and "brāhmaṇāḥ" are used interchangeably, discussed together, and their meaning...
new: In the Veda, when speaking of a thing kept secret from everyone, it is usual to say that it lies hidden in a cave.
basis: Kannada p.572: it is the usage of the Veda to say 'hidden in caves' of secret things (English had an invented 'muktartha' discussion)

old: ...as spoken of here. "**Guhā**" means "guhāyām" (in the hidden place); "**guha**" carries the sense of [something] concealed. In this context, the essence of things not yet understood is spoken of as hidden within the Veda. "**Turīyaṃ**" means the well-known form, that which has come down through generations, [the portion that] is well-established. Some scholars, [regarding the three hidden portions,] hold that what is inaccessible remains genuinely secret, while what is well-known and commonly used is understood as the accepted meaning.
new: Here "**Guhā**" means "guhāyām" (in the cave). Things in a cave are not seen by ordinary people, so it has become usual to say, in speaking of what is secret, that it is in the cave. The fourth part of speech ("turīya") is the part that is current among men.
basis: Kannada p.572

old: **This mantra**, according to the scholarly tradition, is explained differently depending on which of the four categories mentioned in the preceding verse is taken as its subject; and even within our own [Taittiriya-Shakha] tradition, the wise (those who have thoroughly mastered Grammar) understand this mantra by first grasping its true intent through the mind, before articulating it in speech...
new: **This mantra** has been explained by Yaska in the ninth section of the fourth chapter of his Nirukta. As grain (flour) is sifted by winnowing in a winnowing basket, the wise (those who know Grammar) sift speech with the mind (they consider well the nature of words and the like and then speak). By doing so they cultivate friendship with speech (they use good words and speak well). In the words they speak a blessing endowed with right marks resides (their words are well-formed and auspicious)...
basis: Kannada pp.572-573: Yaska explains the mantra in Nirukta 4-9; winnowing simile (English had a statement about the four categories of the preceding verse)

old: ...explaining this fully; thus have the wise elaborated it. Just as [in the analogy given], while looking at her, they know her [that is, understand her true meaning]; from this act of looking arises genuine understanding. This is spoken of as revealed only to those who possess this quality (that is, those able to properly perceive the meaning through Grammar's own light).
new: A man who sees yet does not see, and hears yet does not hear: though he sees with the eye and hears with the ear, he has no knowledge of the meaning of words, so nothing is understood by him; he only pronounces the words, without knowing their meaning. This is said of the man who is not learned. About the learned man the next part says: as a wife, wearing fair garments and adorned with every ornament, comes to her husband out of desire, and the husband looks at her with great regard and speaks to her lovingly, so the Vedas (or words) offer their body, that is, reveal their hidden meaning, to the man learned in the sciences; the learned man can well understand the nature of words and their special meaning. We have already explained the meaning of this Rik at length (see page 528). Therefore Grammar must be studied.
basis: Kannada p.572: the explanation of uta tvah (English had a garbled paragraph about looking at her)

old: Alternatively, deriving it through metathesis (letter-transposition) from the root "√kas" (to move/shine), it may instead convey the sense of "capability" (śakti).
new: Alternatively, deriving it through transposition from the root "√kas", it may convey the sense "opened out, blossomed".
basis: Kannada p.573: kasati, transposed, gives the sense vikasita (opened out); 'capability (shakti)' is not in the Kannada

old: **This mantra**, whether taken as expressing the science of speech (vāk-śāstra), or as describing the structure of grammar (vāk-svarūpa) itself, is a difficult one, requiring the discipline called "grammar" (śabda-śāstra) to properly navigate its path. **Who, then, is capable of understanding it? Only the authorities on Grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra) themselves.**
new: **This mantra** raises the question: what is that road, so hard to travel, to union with speech, that is, to the true nature of speech? It is the path that concerns speech, the science of words (shabda-shastra). **Who knows it? The authorities on Grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra).** Why? Because in the speech of the grammarians the words are well-marked.
basis: Kannada p.573

old: meaning: an auspicious splendor resides upon the speech [of those wise ones]. Since [precisely] the grammatical treatises (vyākaraṇa-śāstra) demonstrate that meaning-bearing forms are present within such words, an auspicious lustre indeed rests upon them.
new: that is, since the words in the speech of the grammarians are well-marked (endowed with the right marks), the auspicious Lakshmi dwells in their speech.
basis: Kannada p.573

old: [here rendered in the mantra as "sruti"]
basis: Kannada p.575 has no such remark; addition removed

old: **"The [portion of the] first-named divisions of words, syllables, and analysis fall into groups... where, in this connection, [the terms] 'gūḍha' [hidden] and 'prasiddha' [well-known] arise; from Śākaṭāyana's own teaching, ten such analyses (nirukta) are in common use — from these, the usage-based tradition."**
new: **"Nighaṇṭu is a well-established name for a book in which groups of synonymous words are chiefly taught; such are the ten Nighaṇṭus (Amarasiṃha, Vaijayantī, Halāyudha and the rest) of common usage."**
basis: Kannada pp.576-577 (embedded translation on p.577): the passage on Nighantu; English paragraph was garbled and mentioned Shakatayana, which is not in the Kannada

old: ending 'apage'

new: So far the necessity of Grammar for understanding the Veda has been explained at length; now the use that is gained from the Nirukta is explained. A work that explains the meaning of words so that the sense is had without the help of another is called Nirukta (nir + ukta): the meaning that arises from a word does not depend on another word. Thus this Nirukta begins with the words "Gauh, gma, jma, kshma, ksha, kshama" and ends with "vasavah, vajinah, devapatnyah, devapatnyah"; for understanding the meaning of words in it no other help (parāpekṣā) is needed, because it is stated clearly in each place that so many words are names of the earth and so many are names of gold.
